doc.title: Ray Drummond interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003

title: The Miles Davis theory of bandleading and future projects
summary: He hires individual voices as Miles did, and lists projects: big band, Mingus, American spirituals, Paul Robeson, with a remark on McCarthy.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: you know you hire people because of their individual voices and you put them together not because you want them to make a sound that you think they should make but because you hear what they do and you want to put them together with the individual voices so that they will interact and make whatever sound comes out of that. And that’s what Miles did. Miles would always do that. Miles was not a person that said I want you to sound like this, I want you to play like this. If anything Miles said, “Uh, you’re not playing enough. I didn’t hire you to sit here and look good, cute and everything, just play, just be yourself.” So that’s the kind of ideal that I’m always striving for. So I guess “Excursion” kind of projects would give me the broadest palette at this point. I’d love to have a big band, some big band projects and whatnot. I did my first big band compositions or arrangements rather a couple of years ago for Lafayette College in Easton and that was fun, it was a challenge to actually do them and so I’d love to do that some more. I mean there’s billions of things. My Mingus project I want to do, my Gospel project — well not Gospel but it’s we talked about spiritual, well American spirituals, I’d like to do, some of them would be black, some of them would be white, some of them would be Native American, some of them might be Asian-American. But tunes considered spirituals or something close to that, where I actually go and re-arrange it and come up with another kind of, actually I got a bunch of ideas for some, I’m a Paul Robeson freak too, I’ve always loved Paul Robeson. There’s a lot of material that he sang and of course his story is completely tragic, certainly it’s a political story for the forties and fifties. Definitely. You want to talk about what McCarthy did?
There’s a perfect example, a commie under every bush and all that silly — now we have a Bush under every commie.
